entries.seminar_title: Barriers to industrial growth and long-run productive efficiency: the role of policy-induced misallocation
entries.speaker: Tianyu Luo
entries.abstract: We study how government-created distortions in upstream coal markets affect capacity investment and productivity in India's electricity industry. The government coal monopoly administratively allocates subsidized coal primarily to inefficient state-owned plants while forcing efficient private generators to purchase coal at market prices often about two times higher. This unequal access distorts not only the allocation of electricity production today, but also incentives to invest in new generating capacity. Using plant-level data for 2006-2017 and detailed administrative records of coal supply contracts, we estimate a dynamic oligopoly model of capacity investment for coal-fired generators. We use the estimated model to study two sets of counterfactuals. Equalizing public-private access to subsidized domestic coal shifts investment towards 2006-2009 (raising it by 4.9 percent), has little effect on aggregate investment, but reallocates production toward more efficient generators. Because the economic value of investment is higher in the early years in our setting, we then consider a counterfactual that provides very generous coal pricing to early private investments but not to later ones. This shifts investment towards 2006-2009 more strongly (raising it by 16.1 percent), thus better mitigating electricity shortages.

entries.speaker: Tan Gan
entries.affiliation: London School of Economics and Political Science
entries.abstract: We study delegation rules by principals uninformed of the underlying state (external uncertainty) and the preferences of better-informed agents (internal uncertainty). Under rich internal uncertainty about the agent’s trade-offs when constrained, making any delegation rule flexible—allowing all compromises between permitted actions—always improves the principal’s worst-case payoff. This provides a rationale for convex delegation sets and, in one dimension, for interval delegation, without imposing parametric assumptions on primitives. Internal uncertainty can justify greater discretion, allowing actions that are never optimal for the principal in any state; and a version of the ally principle holds: alignment along enough dimensions implies unconstrained delegation.

entries.seminar_title: "Great Power Competition or Collusion? The Neoroyalist Future of International Order"
entries.speaker: Stacie Goddard
entries.abstract: With the liberal international order in decline, observers have focused on the likely return to great power competition, with the U.S., China, and Russia mobilizing their resources to counter those of their rivals. But leaders do not seem to be behaving like great power competitors. The actions of the Trump administration, notably, raise a number of significant puzzles for such accounts—the US seems willing to sign deals with traditional adversaries including Russia and China, while targeting long-standing allies like Canada and Denmark. Rather than ready their forces for rivalry, Xi Jinping purges his own military and foreign policy bureaucracy, while Putin gets bogged down in a "forever war" with Ukraine. This talk will suggest that we are seeing, not nineteenth-century dynamics of great power competition, but seventeenth-century processes of great power collusion, a dynamic that threatens to permanently dismantle a liberal international order.
